name: Illusion of Validity
description: A judgment can feel highly convincing because the evidence forms a coherent story, even when its real predictive accuracy is weak. Confidence outruns validity when consistency gets mistaken for proof.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to hiring rubrics, user-research synthesis, forecasting dashboards, AI evaluation, and product bets built on a small but internally coherent body of evidence. A neat narrative can make weak signals feel safer than they are.
prevalence_note: Canonical in Kahneman-adjacent decision-science writing and occasionally invoked in hiring, forecasting, and research-synthesis conversations, but much less common as a named design-practice term than broader overconfidence language.

findings.description: Kahneman and Tversky argue that intuitive predictors often treat coherence among cues as if it guaranteed real predictive power, becoming more confident in a judgment than the evidence warrants. Internal consistency can generate an 'illusion of validity' even when actual predictive accuracy is weak.
